messages.subject: Re: N-micture model
parts:
Dear Wenshuang,

I couldn't open your Zip, so I will try to answer and ask back from what I grasp from your text:
  • can you tell us how many cameras you have in all ? Is it just a single one ?
  • The standard binomial Nmix model of Royle 2004 only allows false negative errors, but NOT false positives. With camera traps usually you don't know how many photographs you make of the same individual (unless you can individually identify them, like for tigers with their stripes), so it is likely that you will count the same individual twice. That means, you double count, and that is a false-positive which is not allowed in this model. So, unless you somehow think you can exclude this possibility, I don't think the binomial Nmix model is adequate for your problem
  • There is a sister model, which is the Poisson-Poisson Nmixture model, which you can fit to the number of detections, regardless of the number of (repeat) detections per individual and occasion. In this sense, this model does allow for false positives and actually in the observation model estimates a detection rate (numbee of detections per individual). However, I think that this model can be very un-robust to violations of its parametric assumptions (the two Poissons). I have seen cases where it has yielded estimates of abundance that were quite unrealistic. But you may try it out and see what it gives.
  • Then, one fundamental limitation of any kind of these Nmixture models is that they are NOT areal-specific. That is, strictly you don't know the area to which your estimates "belong". So, the scaling up from the small areas sampled by the camtraps to the wider, large area is difficult or impossible.
Comments from anybody with more experience with camtraps most welcome !

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: Re: N-micture model
parts:
Dear Wenshuang,

the state model of an N-mixture model in algebra looks like this:

N_i ~ Poisson(lambda_i)

N_i is the realized abundance at site i, and lambda_i is the expected abundance at that site. Without a covariate in the model, lambda will be identical for all sites, but N_i will still be different. You can obtain estimates of N_i using function ranef().

To obtain a (perhaps) better characterization of spatial variability in abundance, you could add covariates into the model for lambda, thus doing something like this:

log(lambda_i) = alpha + beta1 * cov1_i + beta2 * cov2_i ....

If these covariates contain information about spatial variation in abundance, then (1) lambda_i will differ among sites and then represent an adequate measure of site-specific abundance, and (2) presumably the estimates of N_i obtained via ranef() will become better still.

Best regards  -- Marc

thanks for the report. Though your case is of course not a formal test of the model, I nevertheless think that comparisons between estimates and some believed-to-be-known truth in the field can offer some very interesting insight into a model, beyond anything that a simulation study can do.

Couple of comments back:
  1. Yes, the idea is to replace the simulated data with your actual data 🙂 Simulated data just offer a sort of controlled environment within which we can study and understand a statistical model or any other numerical method.
  2. Intuitively, I would NOT aggregate all your data to a single occasion (i.e., T = 1). Though the model can in ideal circumstances be fit with T=1, there is always some loss of information, and I'd just feel better to aggregate the daily raw data perhaps into weekly occasions or some other reasonable duration.   4. It's good to choose inits close to the suspected truth, but I'd also try to run the model without that "initial help" and see whether results still look good (probably they will, but just to check)
  5. I always think we should love but distrust our statistical models. As I said, this model should be particularly distrusted, so you should test it as hard as you can

Dear Wenshuang,

the state model of an N-mixture model in algebra looks like this:

N_i ~ Poisson(lambda_i)

N_i is the realized abundance at site i, and lambda_i is the expected abundance at that site. Without a covariate in the model, lambda will be identical for all sites, but N_i will still be different. You can obtain estimates of N_i using function ranef().

To obtain a (perhaps) better characterization of spatial variability in abundance, you could add covariates into the model for lambda, thus doing something like this:

log(lambda_i) = alpha + beta1 * cov1_i + beta2 * cov2_i ....

If these covariates contain information about spatial variation in abundance, then (1) lambda_i will differ among sites and then represent an adequate measure of site-specific abundance, and (2) presumably the estimates of N_i obtained via ranef() will become better still.

Best regards  -- Marc

I couldn't open your Zip, so I will try to answer and ask back from what I grasp from your text:
  • can you tell us how many cameras you have in all ? Is it just a single one ?
  • The standard binomial Nmix model of Royle 2004 only allows false negative errors, but NOT false positives. With camera traps usually you don't know how many photographs you make of the same individual (unless you can individually identify them, like for tigers with their stripes), so it is likely that you will count the same individual twice. That means, you double count, and that is a false-positive which is not allowed in this model. So, unless you somehow think you can exclude this possibility, I don't think the binomial Nmix model is adequate for your problem
  • There is a sister model, which is the Poisson-Poisson Nmixture model, which you can fit to the number of detections, regardless of the number of (repeat) detections per individual and occasion. In this sense, this model does allow for false positives and actually in the observation model estimates a detection rate (numbee of detections per individual). However, I think that this model can be very un-robust to violations of its parametric assumptions (the two Poissons). I have seen cases where it has yielded estimates of abundance that were quite unrealistic. But you may try it out and see what it gives.
  • Then, one fundamental limitation of any kind of these Nmixture models is that they are NOT areal-specific. That is, strictly you don't know the area to which your estimates "belong". So, the scaling up from the small areas sampled by the camtraps to the wider, large area is difficult or impossible.
Comments from anybody with more experience with camtraps most welcome !

Best regards  --- Marc
